newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Desperate Albanians swarm investment HQ for cash.
newsitem.headline: Desperate Albanians swarm investment HQ for cash.

text.p: Desperate Albanians, financially ruined by fraudulent pyramid investment schemes, rushed to the country's biggest holding company on Thursday after it offered to give back money to thousands of small investors.
From the early hours more than 1,000 people pushed and shoved at the iron fence around the main payout office of the Vefa Holding company, which froze all accounts last month.
"All my family's savings were in these funds," said Mata Leka, 45. "We worked and saved in Greece for four years. We thought all our money was lost, now maybe we'll get something."
But her name was not on the list read out on Thursday.
Albania, Europe's poorest country, has been swept by riots and protests for a month after five fraudulent pyramid schemes went bust, erasing the savings of thousands of Albanians.
Vefa, a household name which boasts 240 businesses and 80,000 investors, froze its client accounts, fearing panic withdrawals after the fraudulent companies collapsed.

On Wednesday Vefa said it would allow small investors with deposits of $5,000 or less to withdraw their money. That could mean paying 48,000 people about $240 million over the next two or three weeks.
Beefy, black-clad guards stood inside the Vefa fence and kept anxious investors at bay on Thursday. The names of about 50 people were read out over a louspeaker.
The crush of people bent the high iron fence and one old woman climbed over into the inner courtyard to the delight of the crowd.
The pyramid scandal has posed the most serious crisis to date for right-wing President Sali Berisha and the government of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi, elected on a free-market ticket in 1992.

Albania emerged from 45 years of ruthless Stalinism and crushing poverty in 1990. There is no real banking system and tens of thousands of people turned to pyramids, which offered interest of 60 percent a month or more.
Leka said her family had put $5,000 in Vefa, and had $4,000 in two failed pyramids - Populli and Xhaferri.
Anila, a student in the crowd, said her family had $5,000 at Vefa and $3,000 in Xhaferri and Gjallica, another failed pyramid scheme based in the southern town of Vlore.
Her parents and brother were working at menial jobs in Greece and had just learned that their savings were lost.
"Frankly, I still don't believe Vefa will pay. We'll just have to wait and see," she said.
Violent protests have swept Albania since the schemes fell in January. Many investors blame the government for failing to regulate the schemes or to warn of their dangers.
Berisha launched a whistle-stop campaign around the Balkan country last week to try to win back support and appease small savers ruined by get-rich-quick schemes.
He has rattled off a string of promises, from removing taxes to faster privatisation but has stood firm so far that the government will not print money to bail out investors.
"We cannot pay their debts but we can intervene to speed up growth and ensure the economic recovery of the people," he told 1,500 supporters in the grimy industrial town of Elbasan.
Berisha and Meksi are faced with the dilemma of printing money to appease investors, and severely damaging the emerging market economy, or holding firm and risking more social unrest.
Berisha is expected to appear at a rally in central Tirana on Thursday to woo the crowd and to commemorate the day the statue of communist dictator Enver Hoxha was toppled in 1991.
